podcast.body: Featured on the brilliant *London Calling* album, this song was written by bass player Paul Simonon. Its sound reflects the influence of "dub music" – "slow, rumbly, bass heavy sounds with a really deep groove" – which The Clash picked up from the Jamaican community living in the Pimlico area of London, their new headquarters.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Paul Simmonon came to write this well-known Clash song, which appeared on the influential album *London Calling*. The song was inspired by the deep bass sounds he absorbed from New Jamaican immigrants. "This is how Paul came to write one of the best known clash songs, Guns of Brixton."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released on December 14, 1979, this track is cited as the prime example of how dub and reggae were integrated into the band's punk rock sound, appearing on their critically acclaimed album, *London Calling*. "The best example of how dub and reggae became part of the punk rock DNA, the song is Guns of Brixton and it was released on December 14, 1979."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Written entirely by Paul Simonon, this song integrated reggae and ska influences into the punk context — reflecting Simonon's Jamaican musical influences — and is one of The Clash's most celebrated tracks. "He wrote 'Guns of Brixton' and integrated sounds of reggae and ska into punk."

podcast.body: This song was directly inspired by the actions of police and rioters in recession-hit Britain during the 1970s. Its creation contributed to The Clash's reputation as leading voices of protest from Britain. "The clash with Guns of Brixton inspired by the actions of police and rioters in recession and Britain in the 1970s."

podcast.body: This was the first track written by bassist Paul Simonon, who struggled with the instrument when the band started. The band decided to let him sing lead on it, despite his nervousness during recording, hoping that the fear he felt about being in the spotlight would translate onto tape, especially with a record executive present in the studio. It is one of the very few songs in The Clash's catalog to feature him on lead vocals. "The first track he wrote was Guns of Brixton and the band decided to give Meshot at seeing it"
